'''James Derek Birchall''' {{post-nominals|FRS|OBE}} (7 October 1930 – 7 December 1995) was an English [[Inorganic chemistry|inorganic chemist]], [[Materials science|materials scientist]], and inventor who spent most of his career working for [[Imperial Chemical Industries]]. He is known for his research on the health effects of exposure to [[silica]] and [[alumina]].<ref name="independent">{{cite news |last1=Kendall |first1=Kevin |title=OBITUARY: Professor Derek Birchall |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/obituary-professor-derek-birchall-1527537.html |accessdate=23 February 2019 |work=[[The Independent]] |date=28 December 1995 |language=en}}</ref>

==Biography==
James Derek Birchall (usually known as Derek) was born in [[Leigh, Greater Manchester|Leigh]], the son of David Birchall, who managed a butcher's shop, and Valetta (née Marsh), who died in childbirth, aged 25. David Birchall remarried four years later, to Dora Mary Leather. In the meantime, Derek had been brought up by his grandparents.

Birchall left primary school, aged 14, and joined an industrial firm in his area, Sutcliffe Speakman<ref>{{Cite web|last=Singleton|first=Allen|title=Sutcliffe Speakman – A century of history|website=Leigh Life|url=https://leigh.life/index.php?page=wiki&id=leighlife:sutcliffe|access-date=3 August 2010}}</ref> as a general laboratory assistant. He was promoted to assistant in the research laboratory, and worked on activated carbon and flame. From an internal company report in 1947 it was evident that Birchall had done a lot of experimental work “with great care and precision”.

After a period of time with John Kerr & Co,<ref>{{Cite web|title=John Kerr and Co|website=Grace's Guide to British Industrial History|url=https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/John_Kerr_and_Co|access-date=5 August 2020}}</ref> and doing his [[Conscription in the United Kingdom|National Service]] in the army, Birchall joined [[Imperial Chemical Industries|ICI]] Salt Division in 1957, as assistant technical officer. Much of his early work there was on the nucleation of [[sodium chloride]] solutions and the improved formation of [[Dendrite (crystal)|dendritic crystals]]. He was then transferred to ICI Cassel Works to apply his expertise to help commission a [[sodium cyanide]] plant, and increase the size of the crystals produced.

After the formation of the Mond Division in 1964, and further promotion, Birchall had his own team and could return to his first love: the extinction of fire. It resulted in the invention and commercialising of Monnex,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Welcome to the home of Monnex™|website=Kerr Fire|url=https://kerrfire.co.uk/|access-date=5 August 2020}}</ref> a dry powder extinguisher still in use today. He later worked on new composite materials, and on silica and its hydrates.
There then followed a period of outside appointments:

* 1976–1985 Visiting Professor in Materials Science, [[University of Surrey]]
* 1977–1979 Visiting Fellow of [[Wolfson College, Oxford]]
* 1984–1986 Visiting Professor at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]]
* 1985 Professorial Associate of [[Brunel University]]
* 1986–1988 Visiting Professor of Biochemistry, University of Surrey
* 1988-ca 1991 Visiting Professor at [[Durham University]]

In 1992, Birchall took up the post of Professor of Inorganic Chemistry at the [[University of Keele]], where he became interested in the role of silicon in biology.

===Awards and honours===

He was named a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] in 1982, making him one of very few individuals without a university degree to be so named. He was named an [[Officer of the Order of the British Empire]] in 1990, and (with J.E. Evetts) was jointly awarded the [[Armourers and Brasiers' Company Prize]] in 1993.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kelly |first1=Anthony |last2=Howard |first2=A. J. |title=James Derek Birchall, O. B. E. 7 October 1930—7 December 1995 |journal=[[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]] |date=November 1997 |volume=43 |pages=89–104 |doi=10.1098/rsbm.1997.0006 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

===Family===

Birchall married Pauline Mary Jones at [[Sheffield]] [[Register office (United Kingdom)|register office]] on 2 June 1956. They had two sons, Shaun and Timothy.

James Derek Birchall died in a traffic accident. He was “struck by a vehicle on a pedestrian crossing in London on 30 November 1995. After several days on a life-support machine he died without regaining consciousness on 7 December.”<ref name= independent/> He was buried at [[St John the Evangelist's Church, Norley]], alongside his wife, who had died five years earlier.
